description_full: Barrick Mining Corporation engages in the exploration, development, production, and sale of mineral properties. It explores for gold, copper, silver, and energy materials. The company was formerly known as Barrick Gold Corporation and changed its name to Barrick Mining Corporation in May 2025. Barrick Mining Corporation was founded in 1983 and is based in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Mark F. Hill B.Eng | Group COO, President, CEO & Director | Age 60 | Compensation: $2.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Barrick Mining Corporation is a large-cap basic materials business with a $61.2B market cap on $10.9B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +34% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +89.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at -1% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $567M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.26× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.
